title: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMPv6) for the Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) Specification
subtitle: How IPv6 nodes report errors and answer a ping.
summary: ICMPv6 is the control-message protocol that every IPv6 node must implement. It carries error reports such as Destination Unreachable, Packet Too Big, Time Exceeded and Parameter Problem, and the Echo Request and Echo Reply pair behind ping. This RFC defines those message formats, the checksum, and the rules that stop error messages from turning into floods. It is an IPv6 Internet Standard (STD 89) and replaces RFC 2463.

plainLanguage.summary: ICMPv6 is the control-message protocol that every IPv6 node must implement. It carries error reports such as Destination Unreachable and Packet Too Big, and the Echo Request and Echo Reply messages behind ping. This RFC defines the message formats, the checksum, and rules that stop error messages from causing floods. It replaces RFC 2463.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 router or host that drops a packet has no way to tell the sender why, and nodes need a basic way to test whether another node is reachable.
tldr.mechanism: Small control messages ride directly inside IPv6 with Next Header 58. Errors (types 0-127) quote the packet that caused them, and informational messages (types 128-255) include Echo Request and Reply.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 depends on ICMPv6 for error reporting, Path MTU Discovery and ping, so every node must implement it and must rate-limit the errors it sends.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IPv4 has the Internet Control Message Protocol from RFC 792. IPv6 uses a revised version called ICMPv6, which this RFC defines. The RFC says it is ICMP "with a number of changes", identified by an IPv6 Next Header value of 58.

ICMPv6 reports errors found while processing packets and performs internet-layer functions such as diagnostics, the "ping" test. The RFC states that it is "an integral part of IPv6" and that the base protocol MUST be fully implemented by every IPv6 node.

The document describes only message formats and the general rules for using them. It does not describe procedures built on top of them, such as Path MTU Discovery, which lives in RFC 1981. Other documents, such as Neighbor Discovery in RFC 2461, add further ICMPv6 message types under the same rules.

RFC 4443 obsoletes RFC 2463 and updates RFC 2780. It was later updated by RFC 4884.
sections.plainLanguage: ICMPv6 is IPv6's version of the Internet Control Message Protocol, identified by Next Header value 58. It reports errors found while processing packets and provides diagnostics such as ping. Every IPv6 node must fully implement it. This RFC defines only message formats and general rules, not procedures built on them.

sections.title: Message Format and Checksum
sections.content:
Every ICMPv6 message sits after an IPv6 header and zero or more extension headers, and the header just before it carries Next Header 58. All messages start with the same three fields: an 8-bit Type, an 8-bit Code and a 16-bit Checksum. The Type decides the format of the rest, and the Code adds a second level of detail.

The high-order bit of the Type splits messages into two classes. A zero means an error message, so types 0 to 127 are errors, and types 128 to 255 are informational messages.

The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the whole ICMPv6 message, computed with the checksum field set to zero and with a pseudo-header of IPv6 fields placed in front. The pseudo-header uses Next Header 58. Including a pseudo-header is a change from IPv4, so the checksum also protects the addresses.

A node with several unicast addresses must pick the message's source address carefully. If it is answering a packet sent to one of its unicast addresses, it uses that same address. If the packet went to a multicast address, an anycast address or an address not belonging to the node, it uses one of its own unicast addresses.

Types 100, 101, 200 and 201 are for private experimentation, and 127 and 255 are reserved for expanding the error and informational ranges.
sections.plainLanguage: Every ICMPv6 message starts with an 8-bit Type, an 8-bit Code and a 16-bit Checksum. Types 0 to 127 are error messages, and types 128 to 255 are informational. The checksum covers the whole message plus a pseudo-header of IPv6 fields, so it also protects the addresses.

sections.title: Error Messages
sections.content:
The RFC defines four error messages. Each one carries 32 bits of type-specific data after the checksum, followed by as much of the offending packet as fits without exceeding the minimum IPv6 MTU. The reply goes to the source address of that offending packet.

Destination Unreachable (1)
Sent when a packet cannot be delivered for reasons other than congestion. Codes 0 to 6 give the reason, from "no route to destination" (0) to "port unreachable" (4) and "reject route" (6).
Packet Too Big (2)
A router MUST send it when a packet is larger than the next link's MTU. The MTU field tells the sender the limit, which feeds Path MTU Discovery.
Time Exceeded (3)
Code 0 means the Hop Limit ran out in transit, which points to a routing loop or too small an initial value. Code 1 means fragment reassembly timed out.
Parameter Problem (4)
A header field was bad. Codes 0, 1 and 2 cover an erroneous field, an unrecognized Next Header and an unrecognized option, and the Pointer gives the octet offset of the problem.

A node receiving any of these MUST pass them to the upper-layer process that sent the original packet, when it can be identified.
sections.plainLanguage: Four error messages exist. Destination Unreachable means a packet could not be delivered for a reason other than congestion. Packet Too Big means a packet exceeds the next link's MTU, the largest size it accepts. Time Exceeded means the hop limit ran out. Parameter Problem means a header field was bad. Each is sent to the source of the offending packet.

sections.title: Echo Request and Echo Reply
sections.content:
The two informational messages defined here make up ping. An Echo Request has Type 128 and an Echo Reply has Type 129. Both use Code 0 and carry a 16-bit Identifier, a 16-bit Sequence Number and optional data.

The Identifier and Sequence Number exist "to aid in matching" replies to requests, and either may be zero. Every node MUST implement the Echo responder function, and SHOULD also provide an application interface for sending requests and receiving replies, such as a ping tool.

The responder must return the data "entirely and unmodified". For a unicast request, the reply's source address MUST be the request's destination address. An Echo Reply SHOULD also be sent for a request to a multicast or anycast address, in which case the source is a unicast address of the interface that received it.

The RFC puts no limit on the amount of data in Echo messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Echo Request (Type 128) and Echo Reply (Type 129) make up ping. They carry an identifier, a sequence number and optional data to match replies to requests. Every node must answer Echo Requests, returning the data unmodified, and should provide a way to send requests.

sections.title: Processing Rules and Rate Limiting
sections.content:
Section 2.4 holds the rules that keep ICMPv6 from making a bad situation worse. An unknown error message MUST be passed to the upper layer, while an unknown informational message MUST be silently discarded. Error messages must quote as much of the offending packet as possible without exceeding the minimum IPv6 MTU.

An error message MUST NOT be sent in response to another ICMPv6 error, to a redirect, to a packet sent to a multicast address, to a link-layer multicast or broadcast packet, or to a packet whose source address does not identify a single node. There are two exceptions to the multicast rule: Packet Too Big, so multicast Path MTU Discovery works, and Parameter Problem Code 2 for an unrecognized option whose type has its highest two bits set to 10.

A node MUST also limit the rate at which it originates errors. The RFC recommends a token bucket and gives example defaults for a small device of B=10 and N=10 per second. A simple timer that permits one error every T milliseconds is called not reasonable, because it breaks bursty tools such as traceroute.

These restrictions "take precedence over any requirement elsewhere in this document" for originating errors.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules keep ICMPv6 from making problems worse. A node must not send an error message in response to another ICMPv6 error, with narrow exceptions for packets sent to multicast addresses. A node must also limit the rate at which it sends errors. Unknown error messages go to the upper layer, and unknown informational messages are discarded.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
ICMPv6 exchanges can be authenticated with the IPv6 Authentication Header, and kept confidential with the Encapsulating Security Payload. The RFC lists attacks such as spoofing the apparent source, redirecting a reply to a different destination, altering message fields, and denial of service by sending a stream of bad packets, which the rate limiting in section 2.4 is meant to blunt.

It singles out one weakness. A malicious node can send a multicast packet with an unknown mandatory destination option, using a real multicast source address. Many receivers then send Parameter Problem messages to that source. The RFC advises multicast sources to be careful with such options.

Because errors are handed up to protocols such as TCP, the RFC also recommends that upper layers validate ICMP messages, using the quoted packet, before acting on them.

For IANA, new Type values come from IETF RFC publication, and new Code values for the types in this document require standards action or IESG approval. The RFC also assigns Destination Unreachable codes 2, 5 and 6 and the experimentation and expansion types noted above.
sections.plainLanguage: ICMPv6 exchanges can be authenticated with the IPv6 Authentication Header and kept confidential with the Encapsulating Security Payload. Listed attacks include spoofed sources, altered messages and denial of service by floods of bad packets. Upper layers such as TCP should validate ICMP messages before acting on them.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Message type. A zero high-order bit marks an error message.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Further detail for the type. Packet Too Big sets it to 0 and the receiver ignores it.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum over a pseudo-header and the whole ICMPv6 message.

fields.name: Type-specific data
fields.desc: Exactly 32 bits of data that depend on the type. Unused fields are set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Invoking packet
fields.desc: As much of the offending packet as fits without the ICMPv6 packet exceeding the minimum IPv6 MTU. Variable length; shown here as the start of that area.

messages.label: Echo Request (128)
messages.note: Carries Identifier, Sequence Number and data.

messages.label: Echo Reply (129)
messages.note: Same Identifier, Sequence Number and data. Source is the request's destination address.

messages.label: Packet with Hop Limit 1
messages.note: The router decrements the Hop Limit to zero and discards the packet.

messages.label: Time Exceeded (3), Code 0
messages.note: Quotes as much of the dropped packet as fits.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: 128 for Echo Request, 129 for Echo Reply.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: ICMPv6 checksum with the IPv6 pseudo-header.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Helps match replies to requests. May be zero. The reply copies it from the request.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Helps match replies to requests. May be zero. The reply copies it from the request.

fields.name: Data
fields.desc: Zero or more octets of arbitrary data, returned entirely and unmodified in the reply. Shown as one row; the real length is variable.

items.title: Never an error about an error
items.text: No error message in response to an ICMPv6 error or redirect.

items.title: Quiet for multicast
items.text: No error for multicast or link-layer multicast and broadcast, except Packet Too Big and Parameter Problem Code 2 with option bits 10.

items.title: Unknown types differ
items.text: Unknown errors go up to the upper layer. Unknown informational messages are silently discarded.

items.title: Rate limit errors
items.text: A token bucket is recommended, for example B=10 and N=10 per second on a small device.

today: ICMPv6 is present on every IPv6 host and router, since the protocol cannot work without it. It underlies the ping and traceroute tools for IPv6 and the Path MTU Discovery that IPv6 depends on, now specified in RFC 8201. The IPv6 core specification has since been replaced by RFC 8200. Firewall operators must let the needed ICMPv6 messages through, which is the subject of RFC 4890.
